metadata.title: Intel's 18A-P chips are in production and just in time as CPU demand ramps up

content.text:
Intel (INTC) announced that its 18A-P process node — a key component to the company's chips and foundry business — has entered initial production. Intel's stock is getting a slight lift in Wednesday trading.
Yahoo Finance Tech Editor Dan Howley dives into the specs of the new hardware and its significance to the AI chipmaker.
Intel, it's beginning its production of its most advanced chip marking a milestone in its ongoing turnaround effort. Tech editor Dan Howley joins me now with more on the chip, which is called 18A, correct?
18A-P.
Oh, excuse me, 18A-P. and like, you know, we don't necessarily always follow the nitty-gritty of like the new chip rollouts.
So, first of all, tell us why this one is so important for Intel.
So, 18A was basically kind of the, uh, I would say the ultimate kind of expression of their turnaround, right? They had been building out these these various nodes, uh, across, I think it was four nodes in five years or five nodes in four years. Um, and that was a huge effort kind of that was put together by Pat Gelsinger, the previous, uh, CEO who was ousted in 2024 and then replaced by Lip-Bu Tan in 2025.
Uh, and that hitting that milestone was massive. Uh, they already have chips out that run on 18A, the Panther Lake chips. You know them in stores as Core Series 3 chips. Uh, in data centers, they're the Xeon 6+ chips. And so this is kind of a permutation of the 18A. This is a more powerful version, more efficient version. Uh, and it would be ideal for, uh, both mobile devices, you know, laptops, things along those lines, and the data center. And so we would see more Intel chips based on this.
Uh, it it really just kind of also serves as proof that that turnaround is, you know, I think nearing the point where you can say, okay, well, we're we're almost past turnaround time, right? Like we're we've steered the ship and now it's going in the right direction. That's how these last two launches really feel. And, you know, it comes as their their data center continues to do well. I mean, uh, in the the prior quarter, what was it? They had 3.93 billion in Q2 last year.
Uh, in the most recent Q2, uh, estimates point to them going to 5.45 billion in the data center. So a huge jump, 38% uh, in revenue. As you pointed out, the stock price has gotten kind of a tailwind to it. Yeah. Uh, massive, some might say, 224% year to date, 476% over the last 12 months. Wow.
That's a little bonkers, but when you think about how uh big the sell-off was for Intel when it was at its worst, you can kind of understand that kind of jump. Although it certainly didn't sell off 40 uh 400 something percent.
Yeah, okay, so let's I'm curious about sort of the next step for Intel because the the big deal about 18A and 18A-P is that these are the first chips um, in this new generation that Intel is making for itself. It's not just designing the chips, like an Nvidia doesn't make its own chips. TSMC makes its chips. Intel is making its own chips.
The next leap that needs to happen, and this is something to your point that Pat Gelsinger really pushed for and it never quite came to fruition, is making these chips for for companies that are not Intel, right? So, like where are we on that?
So there's uh been discussion that they're working with uh a number of of big names. Obviously, there were prior reports uh from Intel that they were working with Microsoft and Amazon. We haven't really heard anything about that as of late, but there have been more recent reports that they're working with, I think the information had reported that they're working with Google and Nvidia. Google apparently is ahead. Uh, they've put in some orders for Intel's So, so basically they, uh, Google has its TPUs.
Mhm.
That's the name of their chips, right? It would be built on this 18A or 18A-P technology. So you have the chip, it's built on this this kind of architecture, uh, and then you put it into a data center. Intel would be the one to put that together.
Uh, Nvidia is still testing to see if they can they can do that with future chips, but that is kind of the goal for Intel is to not just be its own biggest customer for its foundry business. And so in the last quarter, uh they brought in 5.4 billion in revenue, but they had an operating loss of 2.4 billion. So it's not exactly there yet.
Cuz they're still investing in the buildout of all of this stuff.
Exactly.
